title: Classifying German Language Proficiency Levels Using Large Language Models
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of automatic German language proficiency classification using large language models (LLMs). The authors focus on CEFR-level prediction, asking whether prompt engineering, fine-tuning, and probing internal representations can improve classification of learner texts across the full A1–C2 scale.

The approach combines multiple German CEFR-annotated corpora (including Falko and MERLIN) with synthetic A1-level texts generated by Claude 3.5 Sonnet to create a balanced dataset of 1,567 texts. The paper evaluates several LLM-based methods: English and German prompts (zero-shot and few-shot), supervised fine-tuning of LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct with LoRA, and a probing classifier trained on internal activations from LLaMA-3-8B. The work is methodological rather than classroom-based, aimed at language assessment tasks rather than an instructional intervention.

Results show that German prompts outperform English prompts, few-shot prompting improves over zero-shot, probing on internal states performs better than direct prompting, and fine-tuning yields the best performance overall. The fine-tuned model achieves the highest exact accuracy and perfect group accuracy, with errors mostly limited to adjacent CEFR levels. The paper concludes that LLMs can support scalable CEFR assessment, especially when paired with carefully constructed data and model adaptation.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a comparative machine-learning study with a balanced dataset, cross-validation for the probing model, and held-out testing for the fine-tuned model, but it is not an educational impact study and does not use an RCT or QED on learners. Evidence is technically strong for the classification task, but relevance/credibility for K-12 intervention effects is limited.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows moderate-to-strong performance gains for automated CEFR classification, but these are model metrics rather than direct student outcomes. Any educational impact is indirect and limited to assessment efficiency or language-level labeling support rather than demonstrated learner gains.

interventions.use_case: LLM-based automatic classification of German learner texts into CEFR proficiency levels, including prompt engineering, few-shot prompting, fine-tuning LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, and probing of internal representations for proficiency-level prediction
Using Claude 3.5 Sonnet to generate synthetic German learner texts for an A1 CEFR class to augment the classification dataset

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates automated CEFR language-proficiency classification for German learner texts. Performance improved from 23.3% accuracy with an English prompt to 76.7% accuracy and 100.0% group accuracy after fine-tuning LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct on a balanced dataset (n=1,567 texts; weighted F1=0.769).
finding.measure: CEFR level classification accuracy, group accuracy, weighted F1, and mean classification distance on German learner texts

finding.finding_summary: The work argues that LLM-based CEFR classification can support scalable and reliable language assessment, reducing manual effort in scoring proficiency levels. The best fine-tuned model achieved 76.7% exact accuracy and perfect group accuracy, indicating strong potential for automated pre-screening or assistance in assessment workflows.
finding.measure: Classification performance as a proxy for automated assessment usefulness
